focusItems.htmlText:
The Annual Update on OECD Standard-Setting highlights the adoption of eight new or updated legal instruments in the period between the 2025 Ministerial Council Meeting (MCM) and the 2026 MCM (4 June 2025 – 3 June 2026).
While most standard-setting activity focused on updating existing legal instruments, the Recommendation on Quantum Technologies, adopted during the 2026 MCM, was the first intergovernmental standard establishing shared principles and policy guidance for the responsible development and use of trusted quantum technologies.
The Update further details the reports on the implementation, dissemination, and continued relevance of 10 Recommendations which confirm the continuing relevance of said instruments, acknowledge efforts made by Adherents to implement them, and identify implementation gaps.
focusItems.name: 2026 Annual Update on OECD Standard-Setting

focusItems.htmlText:
A report on the implementation, dissemination, and continued relevance of the Recommendation was presented to Council in 2025, assessing the first five years of the Recommendation’s implementation. The Report found that the implementation progress between 2019 and 2024 can be characterised by consolidation, rather than widespread reform. The Recommendation continues to represent best practices. Dissemination of the Recommendation has taken place primarily through the activities of the Competition Committee and the OECD Secretariat. However, specific dissemination by Adherents across and at all levels of government has been limited.

The next reporting to Council is scheduled to take place in 2035.
focusItems.name: Report on the Implementation of the OECD Recommendation Concerning Effective Action against Hard Core Cartels

focusItems.htmlText:
The Report concludes that Respondents have, overall, continued to make progress in implementing the provisions and addressing the principles around the seven major elements of the Recommendation (seismic safety policy, accountability, codes and enforcement, training and qualification, preparedness and planning, community awareness and participation, and risk reduction in new and existing schools). However, persistent gaps remain that hinder full achievement of the Recommendation’s objectives, including the limited integration of seismic hazard data in school site selection, the inconsistent assessment of existing facilities, and the uneven provision of training guidance. To address these challenges, the Report suggests a set of measures that Adherents may consider, including on the seven major elements of the Recommendation.

The next reporting to Council is scheduled to take place in 2035, or earlier if changes in the field warrant it.
focusItems.name: Report on the Implementation of the OECD Recommendation Concerning Guidelines on Earthquake Safety in Schools

focusItems.htmlText:
The Report concludes that Adherents have effectively implemented the Recommendation and describes their substantial and continued efforts to incorporate the arm’s length principle and the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises and Tax Administrations in their transfer pricing systems. With regards to non-Adherents, the Report shows that the OECD Committee on Fiscal Affairs has made significant efforts to either engage or strengthen the dialogue with non-Adherents on transfer pricing issues, which have contributed to expand the adoption of the arm’s length principle by non-Adherents and a broader use of the Guidelines. Finally, the Report concludes that the Recommendation and the Guidelines have been and continue to be of great relevance to Adherents and non-Adherents to preserve an allocation of profits between jurisdictions consistent with the arm’s length principle.

The next reporting to Council is scheduled for 2030 and the Committee on Fiscal Affairs will continue to support Adherents in implementing and disseminating the Recommendation and to foster the dialogue with non-Adherents.
focusItems.name: Report on the Implementation of the OECD Recommendation on the Determination of Transfer Pricing between Associated Enterprises

focusItems.htmlText:
The Report shows a high rate of implementation across Adherents, and concludes on the continued relevance of the Recommendation, while acknowledging a number of recent developments and emerging trends that warrant a revision of the Recommendation. The Report was approved by the Committee on Financial Markets (CMF) on 13 January 2025, and noted and declassified by Council on 18-19 February 2025. The Council invited the CMF to develop a proposal for the Council to revise the Recommendation in light of these developments.

More information on the conclusions of this report are available at this link.
focusItems.name: Report on the Implementation of the OECD Recommendation on Consumer Protection in the field of Consumer Credit

focusItems.htmlText:
The Report finds that Adherents, domestically and in the context of collaborative work at the OECD, have made significant and continued efforts to implement the Recommendation over the past five years, with the Recommendation remaining a dynamic framework, essential for adapting to emerging challenges in nanomaterials safety. At the same time, the Report underscores that challenges remain due to the evolving nature of the field. As a result, regularly updating the Test Guidelines, related Guidance Documents and tools listed in the Annex to the Recommendation will remain an ongoing goal in order for regulatory tools to evolve alongside scientific developments.

The next reporting to Council is scheduled for 2035 and the Chemicals and Biotechnology Committee will continue to support Adherents in implementing the Recommendation.
focusItems.name: Report on the Implementation of the OECD Recommendation on the Safety Testing and Assessment of Manufactured Nanomaterials

focusItems.htmlText:
On 4 June 2025, the Annual Update on OECD Standard-Setting was presented to OECD Ministers at the 2025 Ministerial Council Meeting, providing an overview of the OECD standard-setting work since the last MCM. The report shows how five key policy challenges and priorities identified by Ministers have been translated into concrete actions through 14 new or updated legal instruments covered by the update.  

An overview of the 12 reports prepared on the implementation, dissemination, and continued relevance of OECD Recommendations is also provided, showing how OECD legal instruments have a concrete impact and lead to domestic changes in OECD Members and beyond. The report also identifies improvements to the OECD standard-setting working methods in (i) developing or updating legal instruments, (ii) supporting their dissemination and implementation, as well as (iii) ensuring their continued relevance and impact. The update is also forward-looking as it provides insights as to what will come next, with information on new or updated legal instruments that committees are currently developing (in Annex B) as well as a few examples of planned standard-setting activities on the longer term.
focusItems.name: 2025 Annual Update on OECD Standard-Setting

focusItems.htmlText:
Ahead of the AI Action Summit, a new OECD policy brief highlights how governments can enhance access to and sharing of data and certain AI models, while ensuring privacy and other rights, in line with the Recommendation on Enhancing Access to and Sharing of Data.

Artificial intelligence is transforming economies and societies, but its full potential is hindered by poor access to quality data and models. By breaking down data silos in the context of AI, governments can better:

➡️ Address societal challenges, from environmental issues to global emergencies.
➡️ Boost sustainable growth and social well-being.
➡️ Improve evidence-based policymaking and public service delivery.
➡️ Increase transparency, accountability, and trust.
➡️ Empower users of digital goods and services, including citizens and enterprises.
focusItems.name: Enhancing Access to and Sharing of Data in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

focusItems.htmlText:
To support Adherents in the implementation of the Recommendation, the DAC Network on Governance and its Anti-Corruption Task Team have produced a series of policy briefs taking stock of the rich learning and insights emerging from the first Report on implementation and allowing for deep dives into some of the more complex issues identified.

The three first briefs are now available on the page of the Recommendation: 

  • Corruption as a Development Obstacle 
  • Addressing the under-reporting of suspected incidents of corruption in development co-operation
  • Unpacking the Zero Tolerance to Corruption Principle: Practical implications for development co-operation
focusItems.name: Supporting the implementation of the OECD Recommendation for Development Co-operation Actors on Managing the Risk of Corruption

focusItems.htmlText: This annual update prepared for the 2024 OECD Ministerial Council Meeting presents the new and updated OECD legal instruments adopted by the OECD Council from June 2023 to May 2024. In a changing global context, the OECD has continued to demonstrate its ability to broker consensus and develop or adapt standards proposing innovative solutions to increasingly complex policy issues through a multistakeholder approach.
